title: All Hands 2026 retrospective | Inside Rust Blog
byline:
July 31, 2026 · Nurzhan Saken
     on behalf of the Program team
excerpt: Want to follow along with Rust development? Curious how you might get involved? Take a look!
content_html:
In May 2026, 166 Rustaceans gathered in Utrecht for the Rust All Hands. This event is an opportunity for the Rust Project members and invited guests to work on Rust in person for several days — discuss its future, resolve blockers, build connections between teams, and so on (but not make any final decisions!).

This was the second All Hands organized by RustNL, after the one last year revived the tradition after a six-year hiatus. It was part of RustWeek both times, with the Rust All Hands following directly after the conference days. And yes, the All Hands will happen again in 2027! More details on that at the end.

Also co-located with the All Hands was the RustWeek Unconference, where invited ecosystem maintainers and contributors collaborated with each other and with Rust Project members. This year, there were six participating groups: Bevy Engine, Ariel OS, Linebender, the Safety-Critical Rust Consortium, Rust GPU, and Rust Embedded — with around 60 members in total.

Similarly to last year, the conference day right before the All Hands had a special track, the "Rust Project Track", with talks presented by Project members. (See the recordings.). The talks touched on some of the topics that the Rust teams discussed in greater depth in the All Hands sessions.

Sessions

At the All Hands, there were 73 sessions spread across 3 days and 11 rooms, most of which were pre-scheduled, though some happened spontaneously. You can find the session notes in rust-lang/all-hands-2026.

The State of the Rust teams session kicked off the All Hands and provided a (literal) platform for teams to tell everyone about their activities.

Many sessions focused on pressing topics in the Project's governance. The Leadership Council and Project Directors both held Q&A panels about their roles and processes, and how they relate to one another and the Rust Foundation. The moderation panel provided a safe space for Rust moderators to discuss the challenges they face, with support from Q (head moderator of Hachyderm)1. The Project culture discussion examined sources of disempowerment for maintainers and contributors, and ways to address them. The sessions on Project Goals, north stars, and funding looked at improving how the Project coordinates and communicates work2. Finally, there was a discussion about improving the RFC process, possibly by integrating some ideas from the TC39 process.

As expected, most of the sessions focused on the evolution of Rust itself. The teams discussed a wide variety of efforts, including const generics, const traits, field projections3 and reborrowing4 (1, 2, 3), in-place initialization, SIMD, allocators5, custom lints, stability attributes for libraries, rustc as a library6, the Sized Hierarchy, and auto traits. Beyond these, there were numerous sessions on compiler internals, codegen, semantics, specification, tooling, and infrastructure.

Interoperability was another prominent topic. Discussions covered the overall Rust/C++ interop problem and solution space7, the state of Rust/C++ interop using Crubit8, and safer interop via combining LLVM IR with Rust MIR. It was also great to see in-person collaboration between the Rust Project and both Rust for Linux9 and Rust for CPython, aimed at unblocking further integration of Rust into the Linux kernel and CPython.

Feedback

Overall, people loved the All Hands! Responders rated it 9.5/10 on average, and indicated they'd return next year if given the chance.

Here are some of the things they shared:

Got some very awesome conversations about effects with Jana Dönszelmann and later Tyler Mandry and Benno Lossin which have gotten me very excited and I'm writing blog posts as we speak.

I'm also full of ideas from the mods convo with Q, that I expect to bear fruit in subtle ways.

We may also have unblocked rustc_public, and are working with t-infra to be able to statically compile a rustc driver.

— Nadrieril

The week was full of good surprises! I was surprised at the significant interest in the things I'm working on, based on conversations and the attendance at the workshops (and the related talks).

I was happy to see we're covering most of the high priority interop issues people are concerned about. That was a really good outcome.

There are also a bunch of exciting things in the early stages of discussions or scoping work. Some might never happen, but if/when they are ready, I'm looking forward to sharing them.

— teor

For cargo-semver-checks, we decided on a path forward for building rustdoc JSON with correct features enabled, which is sufficient to unblock cross-crate analysis. We also agreed that it would be desirable to run it on PRs to the standard library, because accidental breakage happens there too and it's extremely painful to deal with. We have a clear path forward here too.

We also got to consensus that it would be good to ship (on stable) a rustup component with the rustdoc JSON of that target triple's standard library, while making the component itself unstable because the JSON format is not stable. This is a fine line, and we technically only just nailed down the details earlier this week, but the bulk of the spicy conversations happened in person.

I have more, these are just the first things that came to mind. I have probably a year and a half's worth of stuff to build off of just things that got unblocked at RustWeek. Now I just need more hours in the day to code! :)

— Predrag Gruevski

In addition to all the value the Rust Project got out of the "official" portions like the talks, All Hands sessions, etc. I also wanted to give one example of "I randomly bumped into someone in the hallway / at the hotel, and learned something invaluable as a result." It was a stroke of good fortune that I happened to bump into the right people, in the right context, to learn about that obscure edge case that will make cargo-semver-checks a more useful tool for the Rust community. This was far from the only such case at the All Hands!

There's inherent value in having people in the same place, and in facilitating opportunities for informal mingling — whether it's in hallways, at the post-event social sessions, at the hotel(s) where many people are staying, etc. I'm thrilled that the organizing team again paid a lot of attention to creating such opportunities in many ways: with the choice of venue, with how the schedule was created, with offering recommended hotel blocks that were relatively close to each other, etc.

— Predrag Gruevski

I covered so many different and varied topics, from meta-dictionary trait solving with lcnr & the rest of t-types over formality discussions with tiif, Xiang & Nico to talking with Aapo about reborrowing and so many more! (Not to mention the huge amount of people I talked with about field projections!) I feel bad making a list, because inevitably I would forget people, because it was so packed!

— Benno Lossin

my highlight on the technical side is definitely that we seem to have finished the non-aliasing-model parts of the opsem. :) specifically, reference and union validity. FCPs are in progress.

We didnt make as much progress on terminology as I had hoped, though we did uncover new interesting questions which is at least some progress.

— Ralf Jung

I'm thrilled that we settled union operational semantics at the All Hands.

I really appreciated the random conversations with people I didn't know. I'm glad that the event provides a low-friction way for Rust team members to make themselves available to others. :heart:

Oh, another one! I loved the "state of the teams" session (thanks to Lori Lorusso for coordinating it). I know it kinda ballooned with the addition of more teams, and I'm glad it did; I loved having a quick overview of the state of many different teams, including teams I haven't had much view into before.

— Josh Triplett

As someone totally new to the Project getting to meet people in person was really good and totally overwhelming but in a good way. I really enjoyed getting to have discussions with so many different people about a variety of rust and non rust topics. I really appreciate and can't thank the team reps enough that not only supported my session but created it (no way it would have worked if you all didn't step up to the stage) and for Mara giving me the opportunity to thank everyone in the closing session. This event and Mara's support did a lot for me and for what my position hopes to achieve.

— Lori Lorusso

Myself being fairly new, I went in not expecting much beyond just wanting to meet everyone, have a good time and watch people do their thing. But I contributed a fair amount to some meetings and had some very nice and productive 1:1 chats. It's also a totally different feeling contributing to rust now when you've met so many people IRL. 100% would do again.

— mejrs

I was at the unconf rather than the all-hands, but I just wanted to say it was a fantastic experience! Having the two events co-located was great for the ability to build connections between ecosystem and project people and work on problems and solutions together. Everyone I interacted with from the project was incredibly friendly and enthusiastic and projected an infectious can-do attitude about making Rust better. As this was my first-time at a Rust event, I came in feeling a bit intimidated about being in the same building as all these brilliant people who have done such impactful work, and I left feeling welcomed, included, and excited for next year.

— Jonathan Keller

All Hands 2027

The Rust All Hands will return next year! It will be part of RustWeek 2027 in Utrecht, the Netherlands, on 27–29 May.

Save the date, and we'll be sharing more information later!

Huge thanks to Mara and RustNL for keeping up this amazing tradition with such a deep level of care.

See you next year!

blocks.html_en: — teor

For cargo-semver-checks, we decided on a path forward for building rustdoc JSON with correct features enabled, which is sufficient to unblock cross-crate analysis. We also agreed that it would be desirable to run it on PRs to the standard library, because accidental breakage happens there too and it's extremely painful to deal with. We have a clear path forward here too.

We also got to consensus that it would be good to ship (on stable) a rustup component with the rustdoc JSON of that target triple's standard library, while making the component itself unstable because the JSON format is not stable. This is a fine line, and we technically only just nailed down the details earlier this week, but the bulk of the spicy conversations happened in person.

I have more, these are just the first things that came to mind. I have probably a year and a half's worth of stuff to build off of just things that got unblocked at RustWeek. Now I just need more hours in the day to code! :)

— Predrag Gruevski

In addition to all the value the Rust Project got out of the "official" portions like the talks, All Hands sessions, etc. I also wanted to give one example of "I randomly bumped into someone in the hallway / at the hotel, and learned something invaluable as a result." It was a stroke of good fortune that I happened to bump into the right people, in the right context, to learn about that obscure edge case that will make cargo-semver-checks a more useful tool for the Rust community. This was far from the only such case at the All Hands!

There's inherent value in having people in the same place, and in facilitating opportunities for informal mingling — whether it's in hallways, at the post-event social sessions, at the hotel(s) where many people are staying, etc. I'm thrilled that the organizing team again paid a lot of attention to creating such opportunities in many ways: with the choice of venue, with how the schedule was created, with offering recommended hotel blocks that were relatively close to each other, etc.

— Predrag Gruevski

content_html_zh:
2026 年 5 月，166 名 Rustaceans 聚集在乌得勒支，参加 Rust All Hands。 这次活动为 Rust 项目成员提供了一个机会，并邀请嘉宾亲自参与 Rust 工作几天——讨论其未来、解决障碍、在团队之间建立联系等等（但不做出任何最终决定！）。

这是 RustNL 组织的第二届全员大会，去年的全员大会在中断六年后恢复了这一传统。 这两次都是 RustWeek 的一部分，Rust All Hands 紧随会议结束后举行。 是的，全体员工大会将于 2027 年再次举行！ 最后有更多详细信息。

与 All Hands 同期举行的还有 RustWeek Unconference，受邀的生态系统维护者和贡献者相互协作，并与 Rust 项目成员协作。 今年，共有六个参与团体：Bevy Engine、Ariel OS、Linebender、Safety-Critical Rust Consortium、Rust GPU 和 Rust Embedded，总共约有 60 名成员。

与去年类似，全员大会之前的会议日有一个特殊的轨道，即“Rust 项目轨道”，由项目成员发表演讲。 （请参阅录音。） 会谈涉及 Rust 团队在全体会议中更深入讨论的一些主题。

会议

在全员大会上，为期 3 天的 11 个会议室共举行了 73 场会议，其中大部分是预先安排的，但也有一些是自发举行的。 您可以在 rust-lang/all-hands-2026 中找到会议笔记。

State of the Rust 团队会议拉开了全员大会的序幕，并为团队提供了一个（字面意义上的）平台，让大家了解他们的活动。

许多会议都集中讨论了项目治理中的紧迫主题。 领导委员会和项目总监都举行了问答小组，讨论他们的角色和流程，以及他们彼此之间以及 Rust 基金会的关系。 在 Q（Hachyderm 的首席版主）1 的支持下，审核小组为 Rust 版主提供了一个安全的空间来讨论他们面临的挑战。 项目文化讨论探讨了维护者和贡献者被剥夺权力的根源以及解决这些问题的方法。 关于项目目标、北极星和资金的会议着眼于改进项目协调和沟通工作的方式2。 最后，讨论了如何改进 RFC 流程，可能通过整合 TC39 流程中的一些想法来实现。

正如预期的那样，大多数会议都集中在 Rust 本身的演变上。 团队讨论了各种各样的工作，包括 const 泛型、const 特征、字段投影 3 和重新借用 4 (1, 2, 3)、就地初始化、SIMD、分配器 5、自定义 lint、库的稳定性属性、rustc 作为库 6、大小层次结构和自动特征。 除此之外，还有许多关于编译器内部结构、代码生成、语义、规范、工具和基础设施的会议。

互操作性是另一个突出的话题。 讨论涵盖了整个 Rust/C++ 互操作问题和解决方案空间7、使用 Crubit8 的 Rust/C++ 互操作状态，以及通过将 LLVM IR 与 Rust MIR 相结合来实现更安全的互操作。 我们也很高兴看到 Rust 项目与 Rust for Linux9 和 Rust for CPython 之间的面对面合作，旨在解锁 Rust 进一步集成到 Linux 内核和 CPython 中。

反馈

总体而言，人们喜欢“全体员工”！ 受访者的平均评分为 9.5/10，并表示如果有机会，他们明年还会再来。

以下是他们分享的一些内容：

与 Jana Dönszelmann 以及后来的 Tyler Mandry 和 Benno Lossin 进行了一些关于效果的非常精彩的对话，这让我非常兴奋，在我们发言时我正在写博客文章。 我也充满了来自 mods convo 与 Q 的想法，我希望这些想法能以微妙的方式结出硕果。 我们可能还解锁了 rustc_public，并且正在与 t-infra 合作，以便能够静态编译 rustc 驱动程序。 — 纳德瑞尔
这一周充满了惊喜！ 根据对话和研讨会（以及相关演讲）的出席情况，我惊讶地发现人们对我正在做的事情表现出浓厚的兴趣。 我很高兴看到我们涵盖了人们关心的大多数高优先级互操作问题。 这确实是一个很好的结果。 在讨论或范围界定工作的早期阶段也有很多令人兴奋的事情。 有些可能永远不会发生，但如果/当它们准备好时，我期待着分享它们。 — 特奥尔
对于 Cargo-semver-checks，我们决定构建 rustdoc JSON 并启用正确功能的前进路径，这足以解锁跨 crate 分析。 我们还同意最好在标准库的 PR 上运行它，因为那里也会发生意外损坏，而且处理起来非常痛苦。 我们在这里也有明确的前进道路。 我们还达成共识，最好使用该目标三元组标准库的 rustdoc JSON 来（稳定）发布 rustup 组件，同时使组件本身不稳定，因为 JSON 格式不稳定。 这是一个微妙的界限，从技术上讲，我们只是在本周早些时候敲定了细节，但大部分激烈的对话都是亲自进行的。 我还有更多，这些只是我首先想到的。 我可能有一年半的时间来构建 RustWeek 上解锁的东西。 现在我只需要一天中有更多时间来编码！ :) — 普雷德拉格鲁耶夫斯基
除了 Rust 项目从“官方”部分（如演讲、全体会议等）中获得的所有价值之外，我还想举一个例子，“我在走廊/酒店随机碰到了某人，并因此学到了一些无价的东西。” 幸运的是，我碰巧在正确的环境中遇到了正确的人，了解了这个模糊的边缘案例，这将使 Cargo-semver-checks 成为 Rust 社区更有用的工具。 这远非全员大会上唯一的此类案例！ 让人们聚集在同一个地方，并促进非正式交往的机会，无论是在走廊、活动后的社交活动、还是多人入住的酒店等，都有其内在的价值。我很高兴组织团队再次非常注重以多种方式创造这样的机会：场地的选择、日程安排的制定方式、提供彼此相对较近的推荐酒店街区等。 — Predrag Gruevski
我涵盖了许多不同的主题，从与 lcnr 和其他 t 类型一起解决元字典特征，与 tiif、Xiang 和 Nico 进行正式讨论，到与 Aapo 讨论重新借用等等！ （更不用说我和很多人谈论过现场预测了！） 我感觉列一个清单很糟糕，因为我不可避免地会忘记人，因为它太拥挤了！ — 本诺·洛辛
我在技术方面的亮点肯定是我们似乎已经完成了 opsem 的非锯齿模型部分。 :) 具体来说，参考和联合有效性。 FCP 正在进行中。 我们在术语方面没有取得我希望的那么多进展，尽管我们确实发现了新的有趣问题，这至少是一些进展。 — 拉尔夫·荣格
我很高兴我们在全体会议上解决了联合操作语义问题。 我真的很欣赏与我不认识的人的随意交谈。 我很高兴该活动为 Rust 团队成员提供了一种低摩擦的方式来向其他人提供帮助。 :heart: 噢，又一个！ 我喜欢“团队状态”会议（感谢 Lori Lorusso 的协调）。 我知道随着更多团队的加入，它的规模有所扩大，我很高兴它做到了；我喜欢快速了解许多不同团队的状态，包括我以前没有太多了解的团队。 — 乔什·特里普利特
作为一个对这个项目完全陌生的人，能够亲自见到人们真的很好，而且完全压倒性的，但是以一种好的方式。 我真的很喜欢与这么多不同的人就各种生锈和非生锈主题进行讨论。 我真的很感激并且无法感谢团队代表，他们不仅支持了我的会议，而且创造了它（如果你们都没有上台的话，它就不可能成功），并且玛拉给了我机会在闭幕会议上感谢每个人。 这次活动和玛拉的支持对我和我的职位希望实现的目标有很大帮助。 — 洛里·洛鲁索
我自己还是个新人，所以我进来时并没有抱太大的期望，只是想认识每个人，玩得开心，看看人们做他们的事情。 但我为一些会议做出了相当大的贡献，并进行了一些非常愉快且富有成效的一对一聊天。 当你在现实生活中遇到这么多人时，导致生锈的感觉也完全不同。 100%会再做一次。 — 梅杰斯
我参加的是非正式会议而不是全体会议，但我只想说这是一次美妙的经历！ 将这两个活动放在同一地点对于在生态系统和项目人员之间建立联系并共同解决问题和解决方案的能力非常有用。 项目中与我互动的每个人都非常友好和热情，并表现出一种富有感染力的进取态度，让 Rust 变得更好。 由于这是我第一次参加 Rust 活动，我进来时感到有点害怕，因为我和所有这些做出了如此有影响力的工作的杰出人士在同一栋楼里，而我离开时感到受到欢迎、包容，并对明年感到兴奋。 — 乔纳森·凯勒
